capabilities.target: Engineering design docs corpus (confidential, write-restricted to engineers)
Chat message routed to the authenticated requesting employee only

inputs.source: Employee question submitted via an SSO-authenticated chat client
Engineering design docs corpus; write access restricted to engineers

instructions.note: The only control against leaking secrets or credentials found in design docs is the prompt instruction 'Never paste secrets or credentials into answers.' This is behavioral and dependent; it provides no protection once an egress-capable tool or an untrusted content source is added.

controls.name: Read-only credential for docs.search
controls.decay_rationale: The credential lacks write, delete, or egress scope; this does not depend on model behavior.

controls.name: No network egress capability exists today
controls.decay_rationale: There is currently no tool capable of moving data outside the trust boundary, so exfiltration is impossible regardless of model behavior. This control is trivially removed the moment an egress-capable tool (for example web.fetch) is added.

controls.name: Chat reply is routed only to the authenticated requester
controls.decay_rationale: The destination is bound to the authenticated session by the chat platform, not chosen by the model.

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or fetch links
controls.decay_rationale: Eliminates render-based side-channel egress (e.g. markdown image exfiltration) regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Only engineers can write to design docs
controls.decay_rationale: Write access to the corpus is enforced outside the model, limiting who can inject content into the retrieval source.

controls.name: Prompt instruction not to paste secrets or credentials
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to withhold sensitive text found in docs; a more capable model, or one following an injected goal, can be argued into including it anyway.

controls.name: Egress allowlist / no-model-controlled-destination constraint for the planned web.fetch tool
controls.decay_rationale: A fixed destination allowlist with no room for model-chosen URLs or query content does not depend on model capability.

controls.name: Provenance tagging and spotlighting for content ingested via the planned Jira MCP server
controls.decay_rationale: Effective if enforced at the MCP boundary as an untrusted tag the model cannot rewrite; only partially dependent because a stronger model could still learn to write believable provenance if tags are model-set.

controls.name: Human approval gate (raw action) before any web.fetch call that follows a confidential docs.search read in the same task
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate does not decay with model capability, though its effectiveness depends on keeping approval volume low.

findings.title: Confidential design-doc content reaches chat replies, but no egress path exists today

attack_path.note: Reads confidential design-doc content into context
Content is authored only by engineers; classified internal
Reply is bound to the same authenticated requester; no external egress capability exists

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'Replies go only to the authenticated requester. The chat client does not render images or fetch links.'
evidence.observation: Destination binding and absence of a rendering side channel keep this path structurally at a limited (S1) sink today.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'There is no network egress today. The credential is read only.'
evidence.observation: No egress-capable capability exists yet, so confidential content cannot leave the trust boundary through this agent today.

recommendations.action: Maintain the current no-egress, read-only posture and require a security review before any tool is added that introduces network egress or ingests external/customer-authored content.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) opens if the planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server (customer tickets) ship without new containment controls

attack_path.note: Confidential engineering content already reachable via cap.docs_search
Reads confidential content into the model's working context on every query
Today's trusted trigger for the read; the planned Jira MCP server would add a new, customer-authored (untrusted) input channel able to reach the same context

Today the only output channel, bound to the requester and non-egress; the planned web.fetch tool (not yet an inventoried capability) would add a genuine egress-capable sink whose destination or query content could be influenced by model output

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest or system prompt diff adding a web.fetch (or similar outbound HTTP) tool; MCP client config diff adding a Jira server whose scope includes customer-filed tickets. Either change alone raises risk; both together complete the lethal trifecta.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'Roadmap for next sprint: add a web.fetch tool so answers can include public references, and connect a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers.'
evidence.observation: Two planned additions together create a classic lethal trifecta: an untrusted source (customer-filed Jira tickets), confidential internal data already reachable via cap.docs_search, and a new egress-capable tool (web.fetch) able to carry data out, for example in a query string.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'There is no network egress today.'
evidence.observation: This is the sole condition preventing exfiltration today; it exists only because no egress tool has been added, not because of a technically enforced boundary that survives the addition of a new tool.
The only planned defense against leaking sensitive content is a behavioral prompt instruction, which is dependent and weakens under model upgrades or injected goals from untrusted ticket content.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, add a strict egress allowlist that excludes any destination whose host, path, or query can be influenced by model output or retrieved content; block requests whose query strings contain doc-derived text.

Treat all content ingested from the Jira MCP server as untrusted (U) input with spotlighting or delimiting; never allow ticket content to alter tool call parameters, such as web.fetch URLs, without human approval.
Require a human approval gate with raw_action review for any web.fetch call made in the same task as a docs.search read of confidential content.
Log and alert on any web.fetch call whose URL or query parameters contain substrings from confidential design docs.

rating.rationale: Reviewed prompt.md and the runtime notes for the docs-qa agent. Today the agent has one read-only, egress-free path: an SSO-authenticated employee's question triggers a confidential-doc read (cap.docs_search) and a reply bound to the same requester (cap.chat_reply), with no untrusted input source and no network egress at all, so inherent and residual risk are low (find.internal_confidential_read_today). The team's own roadmap notes plan to add a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server that ingests customer-filed tickets. Either addition is a documented forecast trigger (new_tool, new_mcp_server) that removes the only control keeping today's risk low, namely the simple absence of any egress-capable tool (ctl.no_network_egress), and introduces a genuinely untrusted (U) input source (customer tickets) alongside data already reachable through cap.docs_search, forming a TC1 lethal trifecta. Projected residual after that change is high, limited only by a weak, dependent prompt instruction against pasting secrets. No structural containment such as an egress allowlist, untrusted-content handling for Jira ticket data, or an approval gate on egress-capable calls is currently planned alongside the rollout.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

No MCP configuration, tool manifest, or IaC was provided for docs.search, the chat reply channel, or the planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server; capability scope, credential scope, and protocol details are inferred from prose runtime notes, so confidence on present-day findings is bounded at high only where the notes are explicit and medium for the forecast finding.

The planned web.fetch and Jira MCP additions are not yet implemented; the forecast finding is necessarily speculative about their exact scope (for example, whether web.fetch will accept model-chosen URLs or query parameters) and should be re-assessed against the actual tool schema and MCP configuration before rollout.
